title: Deborah under the palm (Judges 4–5)
hookLine: a prophet and judge who leads an army and sings the victory song

cards: Between Ramah and Bethel, in the hill country of Ephraim, stands a palm tree with a name: the palm tree of Deborah. People come up to it with their disputes, and a woman sits beneath it and decides them.
The King James says it in one line: "And Deborah, a prophetess, the wife of Lapidoth, she judged Israel at that time." Israel is in the loop again.
A Canaanite king, Jabin, has nine hundred chariots of iron, and the text says he has crushed them for twenty years. His general is Sisera. One day, Deborah sends for a man named Barak.

teach.h: IF THOU WILT GO WITH ME.
teach.b: She tells Barak that God commands him to gather ten thousand men at Mount Tabor, and God will draw Sisera out to meet him.
Barak's answer is honest: "If thou wilt go with me, then I will go: but if thou wilt not go with me, then I will not go." Readers argue over that line. Some hear hesitation.

Others hear a man who knows where God's word comes from, and wants the prophet beside him. Deborah says yes, and adds a twist: the honor won't be his, "for the LORD shall sell Sisera into the hand of a woman."

teach.h: IS NOT THE LORD GONE OUT BEFORE THEE?
teach.b: On the day, she's the one who says go: "Up; for this is the day in which the LORD hath delivered Sisera into thine hand: is not the LORD gone out before thee?"

teach.h: THE WOMAN IN THE PROPHECY IS JAEL.
teach.b: Sisera's army breaks, and Sisera flees on foot to the tent of a woman named Jael, who kills him while he sleeps. So the woman of the prophecy isn't Deborah. It's Jael.
Then, in chapter five, Deborah and Barak sing a fierce poem. The stars fight from heaven; the river Kishon sweeps the enemy away. And in the middle, Deborah names herself.

teach.h: I AROSE A MOTHER IN ISRAEL.
teach.b: The villages had emptied, life on the roads had stopped, "until that I Deborah arose, that I arose a mother in Israel." The chapters never mention children of hers.
She's a mother of a people: the one who got them up and moving again. The Bible calls her prophet and judge and never explains why a woman sits under the palm. She's simply there.

how: Deborah's story is told in Sunday schools and sermons as the story of a prophet and judge of Israel, and churches draw different conclusions from it about women's leadership in church today.

s: the woman who defeats Sisera in the prophecy is Deborah
Sisera dies in the tent of another woman, Jael.
Deborah is called both a prophetess and a judge
Judges 4:4: a prophetess, who judged Israel at that time.
'a mother in Israel' refers to Deborah's own children
the chapters name no children of hers. she is a mother of a people, who got them moving again.

games.q: you're Barak. a prophet tells you God commands you to gather an army against Sisera and his chariots of iron. what do you say?
o: only if you go with me.
games.why: "If thou wilt go with me, then I will go." she goes, and tells him the honor will fall to a woman. it falls to Jael.

practice: Let one woman come to mind who got people up and moving: a grandmother who held a family together, a teacher, a nurse, a coach, the neighbor who organizes everyone.
See her face, and let your gratitude settle on one specific thing she did that nobody thanked her for. If you pray, give thanks for her by name; if you don't, simply hold her in mind.
